- Successors constantly compared to their long-reigning parents
- Difficulty establishing their own identity and authority
- Living in the "shadow" of legendary predecessors

- Governments and institutions adapt to one ruler's style over decades

**3. Legitimacy Deficits:**
- Long reigns create a sense that the previous monarch was uniquely qualified

- Very long reigns can create age gaps between monarch and society
- Successors may have lost touch with contemporary issues

Johann II was the elder son of Aloys II, Prince of Liechtenstein and Countess Franziska Kinsky of Wchinitz and Tettau. He ascended to the throne shortly after his 18th birthday. Until he was surpassed by Elizabeth II on 9 May 2022, his reign had been the longest precisely documented tenure of any European monarch since antiquity in which a regent (that is, a regent serving in place of an underage sovereign) was never employed.[1] Although his mother acted as his regent from 10 February 1859 to November 1860,[2][3] she was not the regent for a minor, but was appointed by her son to fulfil his duties because he wished to finish his education before he began his rule.

**Mahitala Dhibesra Adulyadej Vikrom, the Prince Father**[1] (Template:Lang-th RTGS: **Somdet Phra Mahitalathibet Adunyadetwikrom Phra Borommaratchachanok**, 1 January 1892 – 24 September 1929), formerly **Mahidol Adulyadej, Prince of Songkla** (Template:Lang-th) or **Mahidol Songkla**, was the father of King Ananda Mahidol (Rama VIII) and King Bhumibol Adulyadej (Rama IX) of Thailand, and the paternal grandfather of King Vajiralongkorn (Rama X). He was also regarded as the father of modern medicine and public health in Thailand.
